chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. It starts from points, segments, lines and rays, then builds the angle as a turn, compares angles by laying one over another, and only then measures and draws them in degrees.

points.title: A turn first, a number later
points.text: An angle is first seen as the amount one arm turns about a point, compared by laying angles over each other, and only afterwards given a size in degrees.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's questions, a tool only where handling the angle is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: Fold it, turn it, measure it
points.text: Paper folds make the straight angle, the right angle and a paper protractor, so the numbers on a protractor are understood and not just read.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'longer arms make a bigger angle', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a turn or an overlap, never just a rule.

design_references.text: maths6_ch9 new_design Phase 2 plan: framing intro with one hook, idea topics ending in one doer, optional tool where the manipulation is the idea, a practice topic after each idea topic with one video per book question, one summary topic.

concepts.concept_name: Where do bends and turns hide?

content.text: In this chapter, we will explore some of the most basic ideas of geometry including points, lines, rays, line segments and angles. These ideas form the building blocks of 'plane geometry', and will help us in understanding more advanced topics in geometry such as the construction and analysis of different shapes.

content.text:
1. Look at the dancing figures on the chapter page and at a door, a pair of scissors and your own arm. Before reading on, guess: what do they all do that a plain straight stick does not?
2. Each one has two parts joined at one point, and one part can turn about that point.
3. When the turn is small the parts stay close, and when it is big they open wide. How can we name that turn, compare two of them and measure one? That is what this chapter finds out.

concepts.concept_name: A point and a line segment from a crease

content.text:
Mark a dot on the paper with a sharp tip of a pencil. The sharper the tip, the thinner will be the dot. This tiny dot will give you an idea of a point. A point determines a precise location, but it has no length, breadth or height. Some models for a point are given below.
If you mark three points on a piece of paper, you may be required to distinguish these three points. For this purpose, each of the three points may be denoted by a single capital letter such as Z, P and T. These points are read as 'Point Z', 'Point P' and 'Point T'. Of course, the dots represent precise locations and must be imagined to be invisibly thin.
Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you press a very sharp pencil on paper to make a dot. Does a sharper tip make the dot bigger or smaller?
2. The sharper the tip, the thinner the dot. A point marks an exact place, and we name it with a capital letter such as A or B.
3. Fold a paper and open it. The crease is straight and has two ends, A and B. A straight piece with two end points is a line segment.

concepts.concept_name: The shortest route from A to B

content.text:
Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1).
What is the shortest route from A to B? This shortest path from Point A to Point B (including A and B) as shown here is called the line segment from A to B. It is denoted by either AB (bar over letters) or BA (bar over letters). The points A and B are called the end points of the line segment AB.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you join two points A and B by a zig-zag route, a curved route and a straight route. Which do you think is the shortest?
2. Draw them and compare the lengths. The straight route is the shortest.
3. This shortest path from A to B, including A and B, is the line segment AB.

concepts.concept_name: A line goes on forever

content.text:
Imagine that the line segment from A to B (i.e., AB) is extended beyond A in one direction and beyond B in the other direction without any end (see Fig. 2.2). This is a model for a line. Do you think you can draw a complete picture of a line? No. Why?
A line through two points A and B is written as AB (double-headed arrow over the letters). It extends forever in both directions. Sometimes a line is denoted by a letter like l or m.
Observe that any two points determine a unique line that passes through both of them.

content.text:
Worked example: Imagine that the line segment AB is extended beyond A in one direction and beyond B in the other direction without any end (Fig. 2.2). Do you think you can draw a complete picture of a line? No. Why?
1. A line has no end in either direction.
2. Paper is finite, so we can draw only a part and put arrows at both ends.
Answer: No, because a line goes on forever in both directions, so only a part of it can be drawn (arrowheads show it continues).

concepts.concept_name: A ray starts at a point

content.text:
A ray is a portion of a line that starts at one point (called the starting point or initial point of the ray) and goes on endlessly in a direction. The following are some models for a ray:
Look at the diagram (Fig. 2.3) of a ray. Two points are marked on it. One is the starting point A and the other is a point P on the path of the ray. We then denote the ray by AP (single arrow over the letters).

content.text:
1. Predict first: a torch shines a beam. Does the beam have a start, an end, or both?
2. The beam starts at the torch and goes on in one direction without stopping. A part of a line that starts at one point and goes on one way forever is a ray.
3. We name a ray with the starting point first, so ray TL starts at T and passes through L. Ray LT would start at L.

content.text:
Worked example: A torch at T shines a beam towards a lamp post L. The beam goes past L and never stops. Is the beam a line segment, a ray or a line? Name it.
1. The beam starts at T, a fixed starting point.
2. It passes through L and goes on in one direction without end.
3. A part of a line with one starting point is a ray.
4. The starting point comes first in the name, so the beam is ray TL.
Answer: It is a ray, named TL, with starting point T.

media.description: A zigzag path joins five marked points one after another, and each straight piece between two neighbouring points is named by its end points. Counting the pieces at each marked point shows which points are on one segment and which are on two. A last check counts the pieces from the number of points.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a straight piece between two marked points is a line segment, and a bend is shared by two segments. Watch for students who forget that the two end points of the path belong to only one segment each.

maths_rules: The path goes through the marked points in the order L, M, P, Q, R, and each piece between neighbouring points is straight.

maths_rules: The marked letters on the figure are D, E, O, B and C, so there are five points.

concepts.concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

content.text:
An angle is formed by two rays having a common starting point. Here is an angle formed by rays BD and BE where B is the common starting point (Fig. 2.8).
The point B is called the vertex of the angle, and the rays BD and BE are called the arms of the angle. How can we name this angle? We can simply use the vertex and say that it is the Angle B. To be clearer, we use a point on each of the arms together with the vertex to name the angle. In this case, we name the angle as Angle DBE or Angle EBD. The word angle can be replaced by the symbol '∠', i.e., ∠DBE or ∠EBD. Note that in specifying the angle, the vertex is always written as the middle letter.
To indicate an angle, we use a small curve at the vertex (refer to Fig. 2.9).
Vidya has just opened her book. Let us observe her opening the cover of the book in different scenarios.
Do you see angles being made in each of these cases? Can you mark their arms and vertex?
Let's look at some other examples where angles arise in real life by rotation or turn:
In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects. Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.

content.text:
Worked example: Vidya opens the cover of her book in six cases (Case 1 to Case 6). Do you see angles being made in each of these cases? Can you mark their arms and vertex?
1. The book cover and the page below it form the two arms.
2. The vertex is the hinge where they join.
Answer: Yes, an angle is formed in each case. The arms are the cover and the rest of the book (the two rays along the cover and the book); the vertex is the hinge/spine where they meet.

concepts.concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

content.text:
Worked example: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
1. The two legs are the arms.
2. The joint where they meet is the vertex.
Answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.

concepts.concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

content.text:
Worked example: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects (a stapler, a hinged box, a box with an open flap). Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
1. Find the two parts that turn about a hinge.
2. Those parts are the arms; the hinge is the vertex.
Answer: Each object has two parts joined at a hinge; the two parts are the arms and the hinge is the vertex (e.g., spectacles: a temple (side arm) and the frame; wallet: the two halves; stapler: the top and base; box: lid and box).

concepts.concept_name: An angle is the amount of turn

content.text:
Which angle is greater, the angle in Case 1 or the angle in Case 2?
Just as we talk about the size of a line based on its length, we also talk about the size of an angle based on its amount of rotation.
So, the angle in Case 2 is greater as in this case she needs to rotate the cover more. Similarly, the angle in Case 3 is even larger than that of Case 2, because there is even more rotation, and Cases 4, 5, and 6 are successively larger angles with more and more rotation.
The size of an angle is the amount of rotation or turn that is needed about the vertex to move the first ray to the second ray. (boxed definition with Fig. 2.9)
Do you see how these angles are formed by turning one arm with respect to the other?

interaction_points.answer: In each object the two parts that turn are the arms and the hinge is the vertex. In the spectacles they are the side piece and the frame, and in the wallet they are its two halves

source: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects. Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
video_script.why: The child finds the two arms and the vertex of the angle in common objects that open about a hinge.
video_script.substitution: Draw each of the two parts that turn as a ray that starts at the hinge.
video_script.anchor: a pair of spectacles with a side piece opened, and a wallet opened a little
video_script.wrong_answer: the vertex is the free end of the side piece
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the vertex is the free end of the side piece, the tip behind the ear. The free tip is only where one arm ends, and the arms do not meet there, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The two parts that turn are the arms, and the vertex is the hinge

final_answer.value: In each object the two parts that turn are the arms and the hinge is the vertex. In the spectacles they are the side piece and the frame, and in the wallet they are its two halves
final_answer.spoken: in each object the two parts that turn are the arms and the hinge is the vertex. In the spectacles they are the side piece and the frame, and in the wallet they are its two halves

never_show: the hinge named as the vertex, before the answer beat
maths_rules: An angle is formed by two rays with a common starting point; the rays are the arms and the starting point is the vertex.
In spectacles the side piece and the frame turn about the hinge, so they lie along the two arms.
In a wallet the two halves turn about the place where they are joined, so they lie along the two arms.
The vertex is the one point where both arms start, so in each object it is the hinge.
Slip: the free end of the side piece is only where one arm ends, so it is not the vertex.
video_script.design: One idea: find the hinge, then the two parts that turn there. The spectacles and the wallet stay on the board and open a little. The wrong idea is that the free end of the side piece is the vertex.
open_questions: The worklist answer also lists a stapler, a hinged box and a box with an open flap. The book text names only spectacles and a wallet, so the video uses those two and keeps to the book.

maths_rules: The size of an angle is the amount of rotation, or turn, needed about the vertex to move the first ray to the second ray.
The pages are the first ray and the cover is the second ray, and both start at the hinge.

More turn means a greater angle, so the angle in Case two is greater.
Slip: the length of the cover is the same in both cases, but length does not decide the size of an angle.

maths_rules: An angle has two arms that start at one vertex, and its size is the amount of turn about the vertex.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students mark the two arms and the vertex of the angle in a book cover, a compass, scissors and a hinged object.
Students see that the size of an angle is the amount one arm turns about the vertex, so opening the cover more makes a greater angle.
Students name angles with three letters with the vertex in the middle, find the arms and vertex in pictures, and count the angles formed by three or four points.

concepts.concept_name: 2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q1 (pages 19-20)

content.text:
2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q1 (pages 19-20): Can you find the angles in the given pictures? Draw the rays forming any one of the angles and name the vertex of the angle. (Pictures: a bicycle with points A, B, C, D and arrows marked on it, a wooden crate with slanting slats, a ladder, a bridge.)
1. Pick two lines or parts meeting at a point.
2. Draw them as rays from that point and name the vertex.
Answer: Yes. For example, in the bicycle one angle is ∠BDC with vertex D; one ray is DC and the other ray is DB. Try for other pictures.

concepts.concept_name: 2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q2 (page 20)

content.text:
2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q2 (page 20): Draw and label an angle with arms ST and SR.
1. Mark the vertex S.
2. Draw ray ST and ray SR from S.
3. Mark a small curve between them.
Answer: Draw two rays from S: one through T and one through R, with a curve at S. The angle is ∠RST (or ∠TSR) with vertex S.

concepts.concept_name: 2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q3 (page 20)

content.text:
2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q3 (page 20): Explain why ∠APB cannot be labelled as ∠P. (Figure: vertex P with three rays going through A (upper), B (middle) and C (lower).)
1. At P there are three rays, PA, PB, PC.
2. So there are three different angles at P.
3. ∠P alone cannot tell which one; use points on both arms.
Answer: Three angles share the vertex P (∠APB, ∠BPC and ∠APC). Naming one as ∠P would not say which of them is meant, so we must name a point on each arm.

concepts.concept_name: 2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q5 (page 20)

content.text:
2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q5 (page 20): Mark any three points on your paper that are not on one line. Label them A, B, C. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C? Write them down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9. lines) How many lines? Name them. angles) How many angles using A, B, C?
1. Join each pair of points: AB, BC, CA gives 3 lines.
2. Each point is a vertex of one angle, giving 3 angles.
Answer: Three lines AB, BC, CA and three angles ∠ABC, ∠BCA, ∠CAB.

concepts.concept_name: 2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q6 (page 21)

content.text:
2.5 Angle, Figure it Out Q6 (page 21): Now mark any four points on your paper so that no three of them are on one line. Label them A, B, C, D. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C, D? Write them all down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9. lines) How many lines? Name them. angles) How many angles using A, B, C, D?
1. Pairs of 4 points: 6 lines.
2. At each point the other three points give 3 angles; 4 × 3 = 12 angles.

concepts.concept_name: Comparing by superimposition

content.text:
Look at these animals opening their mouths. Do you see any angles here? If yes, mark the arms and vertex of each one. Some mouths are open wider than others; the more the turning of the jaws, the larger the angle! Can you arrange the angles in this picture from smallest to largest?
Here are some angles. Label each of the angles. How will you compare them?
Draw a few more angles; label them and compare.
Any two angles can be compared by placing them one over the other, i.e., by superimposition. While superimposing, the vertices of the angles must overlap.
After superimposition, it becomes clear which angle is smaller and which is larger.
The picture shows the two angles superimposed. It is now clear that ∠PQR is larger than ∠ABC.

content.text:
Worked example: Look at these animals opening their mouths (snake, fish, bird, crocodile). Do you see any angles here? If yes, mark the arms and vertex of each one. Some mouths are open wider than others; the more the turning of the jaws, the larger the angle! Can you arrange the angles in this picture from smallest to largest?
1. Mark the jaws as arms and the hinge as the vertex.
2. Compare the amounts of opening and order them.
Answer: Yes, each mouth makes an angle (the two jaws are the arms; the hinge of the jaws is the vertex). Arrange them by how wide each mouth is open; the crocodile's looks widest.

concepts.concept_name: Equal angles, whatever the arm length

content.text:
Equal angles. Now consider ∠AOB and ∠XOY in the figure. Which is greater?
The corners of both of these angles match and the arms overlap with each other, i.e., OA and OX, and OB and OY overlap. So, the angles are equal in size.
The reason these angles are considered to be equal in size is because when we visualise each of these angles as being formed out of rotation, we can see that there is an equal amount of rotation needed to move OB to OA and OY to OX.
From the point of view of superimposition, when two angles are superimposed, and the common vertex and the two rays of both angles lie on top of each other, then the sizes of the angles are equal.
Where else do we use superimposition to compare?

concepts.concept_name: Comparing with a transparent circle

content.text:
Two cranes are arguing about who can open their mouth wider, i.e., who is making a bigger angle.
Let us first draw their angles. How do we know which one is bigger? As seen before, one could trace these angles, superimpose them and then check. But can we do it without superimposition?
Suppose we have a transparent circle which can be moved and placed on figures. Can we use this for comparison?
Let us place the circular paper on the angle made by the first crane. The circle is placed in such a way that its centre is on the vertex of the angle. Let us mark the points A and B on the edge circle at the points where the arms of the angle pass through the circle.
Can we use this to find out if this angle is greater than, or equal to or smaller than the angle made by the second crane?
Let us place it on the angle made by the second crane so that the vertex coincides with the centre of the circle and one of the arms passes through OA.
Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
Which crane was making the bigger angle?
If you can make a circular piece of transparent paper, try this method to compare the angles in Fig. 2.10 with each other.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is it always easy to compare two angles by eye? Think of angles of 89° and 91°.
2. Place a transparent circle with its centre on the vertex and mark A and B where the arms cross the circle.
3. Move the circle to the second angle, put one arm through A, and see where the other arm meets the circle compared with B. A point beyond B means a bigger angle.

content.text:
Worked example: Is it always easy to compare two angles?
1. Angles with nearly the same opening look alike.
2. We need superimposition (or measuring) to be sure.
Answer: No. It is not always easy to compare two angles; for example angles of 89 degrees and 91 degrees cannot be compared without measuring or overlapping. For the given figures, comparison is easy.

concepts.concept_name: Comparing with a transparent circle

content.text:
Worked example: A transparent circle is placed on the angle of the first crane with its centre at the vertex; A and B are marked where the arms cross the circle. The circle is then placed on the second crane's angle with the vertex at the centre and one arm through OA. Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
1. Match one arm of each angle with OA.
2. Compare the other end points on the circle (B and Y).
3. A farther end point means a bigger angle.
Answer: Compare where the second arm meets the circle, at Y, with the point B. If Y is beyond B the second angle is bigger, if Y falls on B they are equal, and if Y falls short of B it is smaller. Here Y is very close to B, so the two angles are nearly equal.

concepts.concept_name: Comparing with a transparent circle

content.text:
Worked example: Which crane was making the bigger angle? If you can make a circular piece of transparent paper, try this method to compare the angles in Fig. 2.10 with each other.
1. Place the circle's centre on the vertex of each crane's angle.
2. Mark A and B where the arms cross the circle.
3. Slide the circle to the other angle, keep one arm on OA, and compare where the other arm crosses.
Answer: Trace both beak angles, place the transparent circle on each with its centre on the vertex, mark where the arms cross, and compare the gaps between the marked points on the circle. The crane whose arms are further apart makes the bigger angle.

concepts.concept_name: Pull it together and do it: Which Angle Is Greater?

content.text:
Put the vertices together and one arm over one arm.
The angle whose second arm falls outside is the greater one.
Arm length does not change the size of an angle.

media.description: Four angles with different openings point in different directions. Each angle is labelled with the vertex as the middle letter, one is traced, and the trace is laid over another with the vertices together. Keeko's doubt is that the angle which looks biggest must be the biggest.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: label each angle, then compare by laying one over another with the vertices together and one arm along one arm. Watch for students who pick the angle that merely looks biggest.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

media.title: Which of the two angles is greater?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: when the vertices overlap and both pairs of arms lie on top of each other, the angles are equal. Watch for students who think longer arms make a greater angle.

media.title: What else can be compared by laying one on another?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two line segments are compared with one end of each together, two squares with a corner on a corner, and two circles with the centre on the centre. In each case the shape that sticks out is the larger one. Keeko's doubt is that laying one over another works only for angles.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: superimposition compares any two shapes of the same kind, by matching one common part and seeing which one sticks out. Watch for students who think the method belongs only to angles.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

media.title: Can we always tell which angle is greater by looking?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two angles with very different openings are quick to compare by eye. Two angles with nearly the same opening look alike, so one is laid over the other to be sure. Keeko's doubt is that we can always tell by looking.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: angles with nearly the same opening cannot be compared by eye, so we lay one over the other or measure them. Watch for students who trust their eyes for every pair of angles.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

media.title: Can a circle show which crane's angle is bigger?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A transparent circle is placed on the first crane's angle with its centre on the vertex, and the arms cross its edge at A and B. The circle is moved to the second angle with one arm through A, and the point Y where the other arm crosses is compared with B. Keeko's doubt is that Y not sitting exactly on B means one angle is much bigger.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: on the same circle, the farther the second arm meets the edge from the first arm, the bigger the angle. Watch for students who think any small gap between Y and B means a big difference in the angles.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

concepts.concept_name: 2.6 Comparing Angles, Figure it Out Q1 (page 23)

content.text:
2.6 Comparing Angles, Figure it Out Q1 (page 23): Fold a rectangular sheet of paper, then draw a line along the fold created. Name and compare the angles formed between the fold and the sides of the paper. Make different angles by folding a rectangular sheet of paper and compare the angles. Which is the largest and smallest angle you made?
1. Fold the sheet and mark the crease.
2. Name the four angles between the crease and the sides.
3. Compare by superimposition or folding.
Answer: Example from the book: a slanting crease EF from E on one long side to F on the opposite side gives the angles ∠AEF, ∠BEF, ∠DFE, ∠CFE. ∠AEF and ∠CFE are larger than ∠BEF and ∠DFE. Try more cases; the largest and smallest depend on the folds you make.

content.text:
2.6 Comparing Angles, Figure it Out Q2 (page 23): In each case, determine which angle is greater and why. a. ∠AOB or ∠XOY b. ∠AOB or ∠XOB c. ∠XOB or ∠XOC. Discuss with your friends on how you decided which one is greater. (Figure: O is the vertex; OA is vertical, OX and OY are slanting rays with OX steeper, B and C are on the same horizontal ray, B nearer O.) a) ∠AOB or ∠XOY b) ∠AOB or ∠XOB c) ∠XOB or ∠XOC
1. a) ∠AOB contains ∠XOY inside it, so it is greater.
2. b) ∠XOB lies inside ∠AOB.
3. c) B and C lie on the same ray from O, so the arms are the same.
Answer: a) ∠AOB b) ∠AOB c) neither; they are equal.

concepts.concept_name: Rotating arms and the slit

content.text:
Let us make 'rotating arms' using two paper straws and a paper clip by following these steps:
1. Take two paper straws and a paper clip. 2. Insert the straws into the arms of the paper clip. 3. Your rotating arm is ready!
Make several 'rotating arms' with different angles between the arms. Arrange the angles you have made from smallest to largest by comparing and using superimposition.
Passing through a slit: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles; do not rotate any of the rotating arms during this activity.
Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit as shown below by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms.
Now, shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
The correct one can be found by placing each of the rotating arms over the slit. Let us do this for some of the rotating arms:
Captions: Slit angle is greater than the arms' angle. The arms will not go through the slit. | Slit angle is less than the arms' angle. The arms will not go through the slit. | Slit angle is equal to the arms' angle. The arms will go through the slit.
Only the pair of rotating arms where the angle is equal to that of the slit passes through the slit. Note that the possibility of passing through the slit depends only on the angle between the rotating arms and not on their lengths (as long as they are shorter than the length of the slit).

1. Predict first: two paper straws and a paper clip. Can you make an angle that you can open and close?

concepts.concept_name: Rotating arms and the slit

content.text:
Worked example: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do not rotate any of them). Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms. Now shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
1. Place an arm over the slit.
2. If the slit angle is greater than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
3. If the slit angle is less than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
4. If equal, the arms go through.
Answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).

content.text:
1. Predict first: a girl snips the ends off the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm. Is the angle now smaller?
2. The two arms still meet at the same vertex with the same turn between them, so the angle is unchanged.
3. To reduce the angle, turn one arm towards the other. The size of an angle is the amount of turn, not the length of the arms.

content.text:
Worked example: Challenge: Reduce this angle. (A girl snips the ends of the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm with scissors: 'Angle reduced.' The boy says 'The angle is still the same!')
1. Cutting shortens the arms but the opening stays the same.
2. To reduce the angle, rotate one arm closer to the other.
Answer: Cutting the arms shorter does not change the angle; the size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn between the arms, not on their length. To reduce the angle, bring the arms closer together (turn one arm).

concepts.concept_name: Folding a straight angle in half

content.text:
Let us go back to Vidya's notebook and observe her opening the cover of the book in different scenarios.
She makes a full turn of the cover when she has to write while holding the book in her hand.
She makes a half turn of the cover when she has to open it on her table. In this case, observe the arms of the angle formed. They lie in a straight line. Such an angle is called a straight angle.
Let us consider a straight angle ∠AOB. Observe that any ray OC divides it into two angles, ∠AOC and ∠COB.
Is it possible to draw OC such that the two angles are equal to each other in size?
We can try to solve this problem using a piece of paper. Recall that when a fold is made, it creates a crease which is straight.
Take a rectangular piece of paper and on one of its sides, mark the straight angle AOB. By folding, try to get a line (crease) passing through O that divides ∠AOB into two equal angles.
How can it be done?
Fold the paper such that OB overlaps with OA. Observe the crease and the two angles formed.
Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
Each of these equal angles formed are called right angles. So, a straight angle contains two right angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a straight angle AOB is a half turn. Can a ray OC split it into two equal angles?
2. Mark the straight angle on a paper and fold so that OB lies on OA. The crease through O is OC.
3. The two arms overlap exactly, so the two angles fit on each other and are equal. Folding is the superimposition. Each equal angle is a right angle.

Worked example: Is it possible to draw OC such that the two angles (∠AOC and ∠COB, with ∠AOB a straight angle) are equal to each other in size?
1. Fold so that OB lies on OA.

concepts.concept_name: Folding a straight angle in half

content.text:
Worked example: Take a rectangular piece of paper and on one of its sides, mark the straight angle AOB. By folding, try to get a line (crease) passing through O that divides ∠AOB into two equal angles. How can it be done?
1. Mark A, O, B on one edge.
2. Fold so OB falls on OA.
3. Unfold: the crease through O gives two equal angles.
Answer: Fold the paper so that OB overlaps with OA; the crease through O divides the straight angle into two equal angles.

concepts.concept_name: Folding a straight angle in half

content.text:
Worked example: Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
1. Fold along crease OC.
2. OA and OB coincide, so ∠AOC fits on ∠COB.
3. So they are equal.
Answer: Because OB was folded onto OA, the two arms overlap exactly, so the two angles fit exactly on each other and are equal. Yes, folding itself is the superimposition: fold along the crease and the two angles coincide.

concepts.concept_name: A right angle is a quarter turn

content.text:
If a straight angle is formed by half of a full turn, how much of a full turn will form a right angle?
Observe that a right angle resembles the shape of an 'L'. An angle is a right angle only if it is exactly half of a straight angle. Two lines that meet at right angles are called perpendicular lines.

concepts.concept_name: 2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q1 (page 17)

content.text:
2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q1 (page 17): How many right angles do the windows of your classroom contain? Do you see other right angles in your classroom?
1. Count panes and corners of the window: 4 right angles per rectangular pane.
2. Look for corners of the board, door, desks, books.
Answer: Depends on the classroom (each rectangular window pane has 4 right angles per pane; doors, desks, board corners, book corners are other right angles).

concepts.concept_name: 2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q2 (page 18)

content.text:
2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q2 (page 18): Join A to other grid points in the figure by a straight line to get a straight angle. What are all the different ways of doing it? (Two dot grids of 7 columns by 6 rows. Left grid: A at row 3, column 4 and B at row 3, column 7 joined by a horizontal segment. Right grid: A at row 3, column 3 and B at row 5, column 5, joined by a diagonal segment through the dot at row 4, column 4.) left grid) Join A so that AB makes a straight angle right grid) Join A so that AB makes a straight angle
1. A straight angle needs the new arm in the exact opposite direction from AB.
2. Left: AB goes right, so the new arm goes left: 3 dots (columns 1, 2, 3).
3. Right: AB goes down-right, so the new arm goes up-left: 2 dots.
Answer: Left grid 3 ways, right grid 2 ways: the new segment must lie on the same line as AB, on the opposite side of A.

content.text:
2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q3 (page 18): Now join A to other grid points in the figure by a straight line to get a right angle. What are all the different ways of doing it? Hint: Extend the line further as shown in the figure below. To get a right angle at A, we need to draw a line through it that divides the straight angle CAB into two equal parts. (Same two grids as Q2.) left grid) Join A to grid points so that the new segment is at right angles to AB right grid) Join A to grid points so that the new segment is at right angles to AB
1. Left: AB is horizontal, so the perpendicular is vertical through A: 2 dots above and 3 below.
2. Right: AB moves 1 right and 1 down per step, so the perpendicular moves 1 right and 1 up (or 1 left and 1 down): dots (row 2, col 4), (row 1, col 5), (row 4, col 2), (row 5, col 1).
Answer: Left grid 5 ways, right grid 4 ways (the perpendicular to AB through A, taking every grid dot on it).

concepts.concept_name: 2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q4 (page 19)

content.text:
2.8 Figure it Out (first box) Q4 (page 19): Get a slanting crease on the paper. Now, try to get another crease that is perpendicular to the slanting crease. a. How many right angles do you have now? Justify why the angles are exact right angles. b. Describe how you folded the paper so that any other person who doesn't know the process can simply follow your description to get the right angle. a) How many right angles? Justify. b) Describe how you folded the paper.
1. Fold the slanting crease line onto itself (so the two halves of the crease coincide) to make the perpendicular crease through a point on it.
2. Four equal angles form around the point, each a quarter of a full turn.
Answer: a) Four right angles, each 1/4 of a full turn. b) Open-ended; explore different ways.

concepts.concept_name: Sorting angles by the right angle

content.text:
Angles are classified in three groups as shown below. Right angles are shown in the second group. What could be the common feature of the other two groups?
In the first group, all angles are less than a right angle or in other words, less than a quarter turn. Such angles are called acute angles.
In the third group, all angles are greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle. The turning is more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn. Such angles are called obtuse angles.

2.8 Figure it Out (second box) Q2 (page 19): Make a few acute angles and a few obtuse angles. Draw them in different orientations.

concepts.concept_name: 2.8 Figure it Out (second box) Q3 (page 20)

content.text:
2.8 Figure it Out (second box) Q3 (page 20): Do you know what the words acute and obtuse mean? Acute means sharp and obtuse means blunt. Why do you think these words have been chosen?
1. A small opening makes a sharp point.
2. A large opening makes a blunt shape.
Answer: In acute angles the opening of the edges is less than in obtuse angles, which have larger openings: acute angles look sharp (pointed), obtuse angles look blunt (wide).

content.text:
2.8 Figure it Out (second box) Q4 (page 20): Find out the number of acute angles in each of the figures below. What will be the next figure and how many acute angles will it have? Do you notice any pattern in the numbers? (Figures: (i) one triangle; (ii) the triangle divided into 4 small triangles; (iii) divided into 7 small triangles.) i) Acute angles in the first figure ii) Acute angles in the second figure iii) Acute angles in the third figure next) Next figure
1. All the small triangles are equilateral, so each has 3 acute angles.
2. Number of triangles: 1, 4, 7, 10 gives 3, 12, 21, 30 acute angles.
Answer: 3, 12, 21 and 30 acute angles. Each small triangle has 3 acute angles, and the figures have 1, 4, 7 and 10 small triangles, so the next figure has 30. The numbers go up by 9 each time.

concepts.concept_name: Degrees: 360, 180 and 90

content.text:
We have seen how to compare two angles. But can we actually quantify how big an angle is using a number without having to compare it to another angle?
We saw how various angles can be compared using a circle. Perhaps a circle could be used to assign measures for angles?
To assign precise measures to angles, mathematicians came up with an idea. They divided the angle in the centre of the circle into 360 equal angles or parts. The angle measure of each of these unit parts is 1 degree, which is written as 1°.
This unit part is used to assign measure to any angle: the measure of an angle is the number of 1° unit parts it contains inside it. For example, see this figure:
It contains 30 units of 1° angle and so we say that its angle measure is 30°.
Measures of different angles: What is the measure of a full turn in degrees? As we have taken it to contain 360 degrees, its measure is 360°.
What is the measure of a straight angle in degrees? A straight angle is half of a full turn. As a full-turn is 360°, a half turn is 180°.
What is the measure of a right angle in degrees? Two right angles together form a straight angle. As a straight angle measures 180°, a right angle measures 90°.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a full turn of a circle is cut into 360 equal angles. What would a straight angle, which is half a turn, measure?
2. Each equal part is a unit angle of 1 degree, written 1°. The measure of an angle is the number of 1° parts in it.
3. A full turn is 360°. A straight angle is half of it, 180°, and a right angle is half of that, 90°.

content.text:
Worked example: What is the measure of a straight angle in degrees? What is the measure of a right angle in degrees?
1. A full turn is 360 degrees; a straight angle is half a full turn, so 180 degrees
2. Two right angles form a straight angle, so a right angle is 180 ÷ 2 = 90 degrees
Answer: Straight angle = 180 degrees; right angle = 90 degrees.

concepts.concept_name: Cutting a circle into equal angles

content.text:
A full turn has been divided into 360°. Why 360? The reason why we use 360° today is not fully known. The division of a circle into 360 parts goes back to ancient times. The Rigveda, one of the very oldest texts of humanity going back thousands of years, speaks of a wheel with 360 spokes (Verse 1.164.48). Many ancient calendars, also going back over 3000 years, such as calendars of India, Persia, Babylonia and Egypt, were based on having 360 days in a year. In addition, Babylonian mathematicians frequently used divisions of 60 and 360 due to their use of sexagesimal numbers and counting by 60s.
Perhaps the most important and practical answer for why mathematicians over the years have liked and continued to use 360 degrees is that 360 is the smallest number that can be evenly divided by all numbers up to 10, aside from 7. Thus, one can break up the circle into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10 equal parts, and still have a whole number of degrees in each part! Note that 360 is also evenly divisible by 12, the number of months in a year, and by 24, the number of hours in a day. These facts all make the number 360 very useful.
The circle has been divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 10 and 12 parts below. What are the degree measures of the resulting angles? Write the degree measures down near the indicated angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: cut a circle into 4 equal parts. How many degrees is each angle at the centre?
2. Divide 360 by the number of parts: 360 ÷ 4 = 90, so each is 90°.
3. 360 divides evenly by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12, so it gives whole-number angles for all of these cuts. That is one reason people kept it.

maths_rules: a full turn is divided into 360 equal parts, each part is 1 degree, so a full turn = 360 degrees
a straight angle is half of a full turn: 360 / 2 = 180 degrees
two right angles together form a straight angle, so a right angle is half of a straight angle: 180 / 2 = 90 degrees
check: 90 + 90 = 180 degrees, the straight angle
a straight angle is half a turn, not the whole turn, so it is not 360 degrees

media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A full turn of three hundred and sixty degrees is shared equally among the parts when a circle is cut into one, two, three, four, five, six, eight, nine, ten and twelve parts. Keeko's doubt, that more parts make bigger angles, is broken by comparing a slice of a two part circle with a slice of a twelve part circle.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: equal parts share the full turn equally, so the angle of one part is three hundred and sixty divided by the number of parts. Watch for children who think more parts means a bigger angle.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

concepts.concept_name: Two scales on a protractor

content.text:
How can we measure other angles in degrees? It is for this purpose that we have a tool called a protractor that is either a circle divided into 360 equal parts as shown in Fig. 2.12 (on page 32), or a half circle divided into 180 equal parts.
Here is a protractor. Do you see the straight angle at the center divided into 180 units of 1 degree? Only part of the lines dividing the straight angle are visible, though!
Starting from the marking on the rightmost point of the base, there is a long mark for every 10°. From every such long mark, there is a medium sized mark after 5°.
This is a protractor that you find in your geometry box. It would appear similar to the protractor above except that there are numbers written on it. Will these make it easier to read the angles?
There are two sets of numbers on the protractor: one increasing from right to left and the other increasing from left to right. Why does it include two sets of numbers?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a protractor shows two rows of numbers, one growing left to right and one right to left. Why have both?
2. The marks are 1° units, with a long mark every 10° and a medium one every 5°. You can count in 5s and 10s instead of ones.
3. The two scales let you start from 0 on whichever arm is the base arm, left or right.

content.text:
Worked example: Will these (the numbers written on the protractor) make it easier to read the angles? There are two sets of numbers on the protractor: one increasing from right to left and the other increasing from left to right. Why does it include two sets of numbers?
1. One scale starts at 0 on the right and increases anticlockwise
2. The other starts at 0 on the left and increases clockwise
3. Use the scale whose 0 lies on the arm you chose as the base
Answer: Open-ended. The two scales let you read from either arm as the 0 line (base arm on the right or on the left).

concepts.concept_name: Naming angles and reading them by subtracting

content.text:
Worked example: Did you include angles such as ∠TOQ? Which set of markings did you use, inner or outer? What is the measure of ∠TOS?
1. ∠TOQ = ∠QOT = 125°
2. ∠TOS = ∠SOT = 35°
Answer: ∠TOQ = 125° (same as ∠QOT). ∠TOS = 35° (same as ∠SOT). Either scale works if it is read from the same 0 arm.

concepts.concept_name: Naming angles and reading them by subtracting

content.text:
Worked example: Can you use the numbers marked to find the angle without counting the number of markings? Here, OT and OS pass through the numbers 20 and 55 on the outer scale. How many units of 1 degree are contained between these two arms? Can subtraction be used here?
1. Read both arms on the same (outer) scale: 20 and 55
2. Subtract: 55 − 20 gives 35 degrees
Answer: Yes. 55 − 20 gives 35 units, so the angle between OT and OS is 35°. Yes, subtraction can be used.

media.title: How do we find every angle between the rays on a protractor?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Six rays leave the centre of a protractor, and the scale that starts at zero on the first ray gives a reading for each of the others. media.title: Can subtraction give an angle without counting the marks?

content.text:
Figure it out (after Unlabelled protractor), Q1: Write the measures of the following angles: a. ∠KAL b. ∠WAL c. ∠TAK. Answer: a. ∠KAL = 30°, b. ∠WAL = 50°, c. ∠TAK = 120°. Yes, it is possible to count in 5s or 10s.

concepts.concept_name: Half a circle and a quarter: 180° and 90°

content.text:
You may have wondered how the different equally spaced markings are made on a protractor. We will now see how we can make some of them!
1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle (Fig. 2.13). A circle or one full turn is 360°.
2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle.
The measure of half a circle is 1/2 of a full turn. (Fig. 2.14) So, the measure of half a turn = 1/2 of ____ = 180°. Thus, write 180° in the left bottom corner of the semicircle.
3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half as shown in Fig. 2.15 to form a quarter circle.
The measure of a quarter circle is 1/4 of a full turn. The measure of a 1/4 turn = 1/4 of 360° is ______. Or, the measure of a 1/4 turn = 1/2 of a half turn = 1/2 of 180° is ______. Thus, mark 90° at the top of the semicircle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you fold a paper circle in half. Which angle does the half circle show at its centre?
2. A full turn is 360°, so half a turn is half of 360° and measures 180°.
3. Fold the semicircle in half to get a quarter circle. A quarter of 360° is 90°, and half of 180° is also 90°, so write 90° at the top.

content.text:
Worked example: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle (Fig. 2.13). A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half as shown in Fig. 2.15 to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again as shown in Figs. 2.16 and 2.17. 5. Continue with another half fold as shown in Fig. 2.18. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc., as shown in Fig. 2.19 and Fig. 2.20.
1. Circle = 360°; half fold gives 180° (write 180° at left bottom corner)
2. Quarter circle gives 90° (mark at top)
3. Next fold gives 45° and 135°
4. Next fold gives 22.5°, 67.5°, 112.5°, 157.5°
Answer: Open-ended craft. Resulting marks on the semicircle: 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°, 112.5°, 135°, 157.5°, 180°.

items: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle. A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again. 5. Continue with another half fold. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc. (2.9 Make your own protractor, pages 37 to 39)

media.description: An angle bisector is a crease that cuts an angle into two equal angles, and the creases OE and OC of the paper protractor are bisectors, checked by folding. Keeko's doubt, that a bisector can cut an angle into parts of any size, is broken by folding along an unequal crease.

content.text:
Figure it Out (after Angle Bisector), Q4: How can you find the degree measure of the angle given below using a protractor?
1. Measure the unmarked angle = 100°
2. Marked angle = 360° − 100° = 260°
Answer: The marked angle is a reflex angle: measure the unmarked angle (100°) and subtract from 360°: 360° − 100° = 260°. (Book also says: try other ways to find the marked angle.)

2. Marked angle = 360° − 100° = 260°
Answer: The marked angle is a reflex angle: measure the unmarked angle (100°) and subtract from 360°: 360° − 100° = 260°. (Book also says: try other ways to find the marked angle.)

concepts.concept_name: The clock as a full turn

content.text:
Where are the angles?
1. Angles in a clock: a. The hands of a clock make different angles at different times. At 1 o'clock, the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b. What will be the angle at 2 o'clock? And at 4 o'clock? 6 o'clock? c. Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the hands of a clock make an angle at 5 o'clock. How many degrees is it?
2. The 12 hours cut the full turn of 360° into 12 equal parts, so each hour is 360 ÷ 12 = 30°.
3. At 5 o'clock the hands are 5 hours apart, so the angle is 5 × 30 = 150°.

steps: Predict first: the hands of a clock make an angle at 5 o'clock. How many degrees is it?

content.text:
Worked example: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 5 o'clock?
1. A full turn of the clock face is 360 degrees and it has 12 hours, so one hour is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees.
2. At 5 o'clock the hands are 5 hours apart, so the angle is 5 × 30 = 150 degrees.
Answer: 150 degrees

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q1: Angles in a clock: a. The hands of a clock make different angles at different times. At 1 o'clock, the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b. What will be the angle at 2 o'clock? And at 4 o'clock? 6 o'clock? c. Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock. a) At 1 o'clock the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b) Angle at 2, 4 and 6 o'clock c) Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock
Answer: a. The clock's 360° is divided into 12 equal parts, so the angle between two successive numbers is 360/12 = 30°. b. 2 o'clock = 60°, 4 o'clock = 120°, 6 o'clock = 180°. c. e.g. 3 o'clock = 90°, 9 o'clock = 270°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q2: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?
Answer: Yes. The vertex is the point where the door meets the wall (the hinge); the arms are the edge of the door and the wall.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q3: Vidya is enjoying her time on the swing. She notices that the greater the angle with which she starts the swinging, the greater is the speed she achieves on her swing. But where is the angle? Are you able to see any angle?
Answer: The angle is not drawn, but fix one arm at the position where she starts swinging (initial position); the angle is between that position and the position where she attains the greatest swing on one side.

content.answer: The angle is not drawn, but fix one arm at the position where she starts swinging (initial position); the angle is between that position and the position where she attains the greatest swing on one side.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q4: Here is a toy with slanting slabs attached to its sides; the greater the angles or slopes of the slabs, the faster the balls roll. Can angles be used to describe the slopes of the slabs? What are the arms of each angle? Which arm is visible and which is not?
Answer: Yes, a larger angle means a greater slope. The edges of the slabs are arms of the angles; the top horizontal ray is not visible, the slab edges are.

content.text:

media.title: Why is the clock angle thirty degrees at one o'clock?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The book says that the hands of a clock make thirty degrees at one o'clock. The angle of one gap is found by sharing the full turn into twelve equal gaps, and the angles at other hours come from counting the gaps between the hands.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the angle between the hands is the number of gaps between them times thirty degrees. Watch for students who forget that the hands make two angles that together fill the full turn.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

interaction_points.prompt: Why is it thirty degrees?
interaction_points.answer: 30° = 360° ÷ 12; 2 o'clock 60°, 4 o'clock 120°, 6 o'clock 180°; also 3 o'clock 90°, 9 o'clock 270°

final_answer.value: 30° = 360° ÷ 12; 2 o'clock 60°, 4 o'clock 120°, 6 o'clock 180°; also 3 o'clock 90°, 9 o'clock 270°
final_answer.spoken: two o'clock sixty degrees, four o'clock one hundred and twenty degrees, six o'clock one hundred and eighty degrees

maths_rules: a full turn of the clock face = 360 degrees, cut into 12 equal gaps
one gap = 360 / 12 = 30 degrees, so one o'clock gives 30 degrees
two o'clock: 2 x 30 = 60 degrees
four o'clock: 4 x 30 = 120 degrees
six o'clock: 6 x 30 = 180 degrees, a straight angle
three o'clock: 3 x 30 = 90 degrees
nine o'clock: 9 x 30 = 270 degrees one way round, and 3 x 30 = 90 degrees the other way; 90 + 270 = 360
check: the angle one way and the angle the other way add up to 360 degrees
video_script.design: The clock face stays on the board. The angle of one gap is found first, then the gaps are counted for each hour, and the angles are held back until the answer line.
open_questions: The book gives 270 degrees for nine o'clock, which is the angle the long way round. The angle between the hands is usually taken as 90 degrees, the short way, so the video says both and that they add up to a full turn.

media.title: Can the opening of a door be an angle?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A door fixed to a wall can be open a little or a lot. The place where the door turns, and the two lines that make the opening, are found, to see whether the opening is an angle with a vertex and two arms.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the opening of a door is an angle whose vertex is where the door meets the wall and whose arms are the edge of the door and the wall. Watch for students who take the floor or the doorway as an arm.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

concepts.concept_name: Drawing a 30° angle

content.text:
Vidya wants to draw a 30° angle and name it ∠TIN using a protractor.
In ∠TIN, I will be the vertex, IT and IN will be the arms of the angle. Keeping one arm, say IN, as the reference (base), the other arm IT should take a turn of 30°.
Step 1: We begin with the base and draw ray IN:
Step 2: We will place the centre point of the protractor on I and align IN to the 0 line.
Step 3: Now, starting from 0, count your degrees (0, 10, 30) up to 30 on the protractor. Mark point T at the label 30°.
Step 4: Using a ruler join the point I and T. ∠TIN = 30° is the required angle.

concepts.concept_name: Angle guessing games

content.text:
This is an angle guessing game! Play this game with your classmates by making two teams, Team 1 and Team 2. Here are the instructions and rules for the game:
Team 1 secretly choose an angle measure, for example, 49° and makes an angle with that measure using a protractor without Team 2 being able to see it.
Team 2 now gets to look at the angle. They have to quickly discuss and guess the number of degrees in the angle (without using a protractor!).
Team 1 now demonstrates the true measure of the angle with a protractor.
Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between their guess and the correct measure. For example, if Team 2 guesses 39°, then they score 10 points (49° to 39°).
Each team gets five turns. The winner is the team with the lowest score!
We now change the rules of the game a bit. Play this game with your classmates by again making two teams, Team 1 and Team 2. Here are the instructions and rules:
Team 1 announces to all, an angle measure, e.g., 34°.
A player from Team 2 must draw that angle on the board without using a protractor. Other members of Team 2 can help the player by speaking words like 'Make it bigger!' or 'Make it smaller!'.
A player from Team 1 measures the angle with a protractor for all to see.
Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between Team 2's angle size and the intended angle size. For example, if player's angle from Team 2 is measured to be 25°, then Team 2 scores 9 points (34° to 25°).
Each team gets five turns. The winner is again the team with the lowest score.
Teacher's Note: These games are important to play to build intuition about angles and their measures. Return to this game at least once or twice on different days to build practice in estimating angles. Note that these games can also be played between pairs of students.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Team 1 draws an angle without showing it. Can Team 2 guess within a few degrees?
2. Guess, measure with the protractor, and score by how close you were. Closer guesses score more.
3. Keep the benchmark angles in mind: a right angle is 90°, half of it is 45°, and a straight angle is 180°. Guessing is practice for the eye, and the protractor gives the exact number.

media.title: How far off is an angle guess?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: In a guessing game, one team makes a secret angle and the other team guesses its size. The true size is read with a protractor, and the smaller number is taken from the bigger number to find how far off the guess was. Keeko thinks guessing is pointless when a protractor is there.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: how far off a guess is equals the bigger number minus the smaller number, whichever of the two is bigger. Watch for students who subtract the true size from the guess even when the guess is smaller.

Figure it Out, Q1: In Fig. 2.23, list all the angles possible. Did you find them all? Now, guess the measures of all the angles. Then, measure the angles with a protractor. Record all your numbers in a table. See how close your guesses are to the actual measures.
1. List every angle formed by the segments
2. Guess its measure
3. Measure with the protractor and record in a table

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q2: Use a protractor to draw angles having the following degree measures: a. 110° b. 40° c. 75° d. 112° e. 134° a) 110° b) 40° c) 75° d) 112° e) 134°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q3: Draw an angle whose degree measure is the same as the angle given below. Also, write down the steps you followed to draw the angle.
1. Measure ∠IHJ with the protractor
2. Draw a base ray, place the protractor centre on its end and align it with 0
3. Mark the measure and join to the vertex
4. Write down these steps
Answer: Measure ∠IHJ with a protractor, then draw an angle of that measure following the steps of the 30° example (about 40 degrees by eye from the picture).

media.title: How do we find every angle in a figure?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A figure of many lines hides many angles. Each place where lines meet is checked, the rays that start there are paired up, and each angle is named with three letters. Each angle is then guessed, measured and recorded in a table.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: look at each place where lines meet, pair up the rays that start there, and name every pair with the vertex letter in the middle. Watch for students who stop after the first few angles, since the book says to try more.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

media.context: Lines and Angles. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Five angles of different sizes are drawn with a protractor. For each one, the centre goes on the vertex, the base ray lies on a zero line, and the degrees are counted from that zero up to the size needed.

media.title: How do we copy an angle with a protractor?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A given angle is measured with a protractor, and a new angle with the same number of degrees is drawn from a fresh base ray. The new angle is measured again as a check, and the steps are written down.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: to copy an angle, first measure it, then draw a new angle with that number of degrees. Watch for students who copy the angle by eye and do not measure it.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

concepts.concept_name: Naming an angle from its degrees

content.text:
We have read about different types of angles in this chapter. We have seen that a straight angle is 180° and a right angle is 90°. How can other types of angles, acute and obtuse, be described in terms of their degree measures?
Acute Angle: Angles that are smaller than the right angle, i.e., less than 90° and are greater than 0°, are called acute angles.
Obtuse Angle: Angles that are greater than the right angle and less than the straight angle, i.e., greater than 90° and less than 180°, are called obtuse angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an angle measures 120°. Is it acute, right or obtuse?
2. Compare the measure with 90° and 180°. Less than 90° is acute, exactly 90° is right, and more than 90° and less than 180° is obtuse.
3. 90° is right and not obtuse, and 180° is a straight angle.

content.text:
Worked example: Name each angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight: 35°, 90°, 120°, 180°.
1. 35° is less than 90°, so it is acute.
2. 90° is exactly a quarter turn, so it is a right angle.
3. 120° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
4. 180° is a half turn, so it is a straight angle.
Answer: 35° is acute, 90° is right, 120° is obtuse and 180° is straight.

concepts.concept_name: The reflex angle

content.text:
Have we covered all the possible measures that an angle can take? Here is another type of angle.
Reflex angle: Angles that are greater than the straight angle and less than the whole angle, i.e., greater than 180° and less than 360°, are called reflex angles.
content.publication_text:

lines: Have we covered all the possible measures that an angle can take? Here is another type of angle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an angle opens past a straight angle. What do we call it, and how can we measure it with a protractor that stops at 180°?
2. An angle of more than 180° and less than 360° is a reflex angle.
3. Measure the smaller angle on the other side and take it from a full turn. If it is 100°, the reflex angle is 360 − 100 gives 260°.

2. The reflex angle is 360 − 100 gives 260 degrees.
Answer: 260 degrees

concepts.concept_name: Angles that add up to a straight angle

content.text:
In this figure, ∠TER = 80°. What is the measure of ∠BET? What is the measure of ∠SET?
Hint: Observe that ∠REB is a straight angle. Hence, the degree measure of ∠REB = 180° of which 80° is covered by ∠TER. A similar argument can be applied to find the measure of ∠SET.

1. Predict first: ∠TER is 80° and the line BER is straight. What is ∠BET?
2. A straight angle is 180°, and the two angles make it up together.
3. Subtract: 180 − 80 gives 100°. So ∠BET is 100°, which is obtuse.

content.text:
Worked example: In this figure, ∠TER = 80°. What is the measure of ∠BET? What is the measure of ∠SET? (Hint: Observe that ∠REB is a straight angle. Hence, the degree measure of ∠REB = 180° of which 80° is covered by ∠TER. A similar argument can be applied to find the measure of ∠SET.)
1. ∠BET = 180° − 80° = 100°
2. ∠SER = 90° (shown), so ∠SET = 90° − 80° = 10°
Answer: ∠BET = 100°, ∠SET = 10°.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students name an angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight by comparing its measure with 90 and 180.
Students say that an angle bigger than a straight angle and less than a full turn is reflex, and find its measure from the part of the turn that is left.
Students use the 180° straight angle to find an unknown neighbouring angle by subtracting the given one.
Students measure or estimate angles, classify each, draw angles of given sizes and build figures and letters from angle clues.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out box 2, Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out box 2, Q6: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes. What is the degree measure of the angle between two spokes next to each other? What is the largest acute angle formed between two spokes?

2. Multiples of 15 below 90 are 15, 30, 45, 60, 75; the largest is 75
Answer: 15° between neighbouring spokes; the largest acute angle between two spokes is 75°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out box 2, Q7, Puzzle

content.text:
Figure it Out box 2, Q7, Puzzle: Puzzle: I am an acute angle. If you double my measure, you get an acute angle. If you triple my measure, you will get an acute angle again. If you quadruple (four times) my measure, you will get an acute angle yet again! But if you multiply my measure by 5, you will get an obtuse angle measure. What are the possibilities for my measure?
1. 4 × measure < 90, so measure < 22.5
2. 5 × measure > 90, so measure > 18
3. Whole degrees between 18 and 22.5: 19, 20, 21, 22
Answer: The acute angle can be 19°, 20°, 21° and 22° (whole-number degrees).

media.title: What is the angle between two spokes of the wheel?
media.context: Lines and Angles. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Twenty four equal gaps fill a full turn of three hundred sixty degrees, so one gap is fifteen degrees. Two spokes that are some gaps apart make that many fifteens, and the largest one under ninety is seventy five degrees.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: equal gaps share the full turn, and an angle between any two spokes is a count of gaps times the gap angle. Watch for students who count ninety degrees as acute.

concepts.concept_name: Lines and angles: the whole chapter

content.text:
A point determines a location. It is denoted by a capital letter.
A line segment corresponds to the shortest distance between two points. The line segment joining points S and T is denoted by ST (with a bar over it).
A line is obtained when a line segment like ST is extended on both sides indefinitely; it is denoted by ST (with a double arrow over it) or sometimes by a single small letter like m.
A ray is a portion of a line starting at a point D and going in one direction indefinitely. It is denoted by DP (with an arrow over it) where P is another point on the ray.
An angle can be visualised as two rays starting from a common starting point. Two rays OP and OM form the angle ∠POM (also called ∠MOP); here, O is called the vertex of the angle, and the rays OP and OM are called the arms of the angle.
The size of an angle is the amount of rotation or turn needed about the vertex to rotate one ray of the angle onto the other ray of the angle.
The sizes of angles can be measured in degrees. One full rotation or turn is considered as 360 degrees and denoted as 360°.
Degree measures of angles can be measured using a protractor.
Angles can be straight (180°), right (90°), acute (more than 0° and less than 90°), obtuse (more than 90° and less than 180°), and reflex (more than 180° and less than 360°).

content.text:
1. Predict first: a line, a ray and a segment all lie along the same path. How do they differ?
2. A segment has two ends, a ray has one end, and a line has none. An angle is the turn between two rays at a vertex, and its measure is in degrees: 90° is a right angle, and 360° is a full turn.
3. Still open for you: can you draw an angle of 135° and name its type before you measure it?
