learning_objectives.objective_text: Students recall how lines, rays and angles are named, how an angle is measured and drawn, and what each type of angle is.

objectives.objective_text: Students mark a point with a sharp pencil tip, label the dot with a capital letter, and see a folded crease as a line segment with two end points.
Students compare routes between two points and conclude that the straight one is the shortest and is the line segment AB.
Students recall that a point marks an exact place and that the line segment is the shortest path between two points, and give an example of each from around them.
Students explain why a complete line cannot be drawn, say that two points fix exactly one line, and name a line through two points.
Students recognise a ray as a part of a line with one starting point, and write its name with the starting point first.
Students name the points, line segments, rays and lines in a figure, draw a figure from a description, and say whether two names of a ray are the same.
Students mark the two arms and the vertex of the angle in a book cover, a compass, scissors and a hinged object.
Students see that the size of an angle is the amount one arm turns about the vertex, so opening the cover more makes a greater angle.
Students name angles with three letters with the vertex in the middle, find the arms and vertex in pictures, and count the angles formed by three or four points.
Students compare two labelled angles by placing one over the other with the vertices together and one arm over one arm.
Students see that two angles are equal when they fit exactly on each other, and use the idea to compare other things.
Students place a transparent circle on an angle, mark where the arms cross it, and compare two angles by where the second arm meets the circle.
Students drag one angle over another on the tool, say which is greater or whether they are equal, and give a reason.
Students make rotating arms, order them by superimposition, and find the one that passes through a slit of the same angle.
Students explain why snipping the ends of the arms leaves an angle unchanged, and say how to really reduce it.
Students explain that the size of an angle is the turn between the arms and use a rotating arm to match an angle, whatever the length of the arms.
Students fold a straight angle so that its two arms overlap, and explain why the two angles formed are equal.
Students say that a right angle is a quarter of a full turn, and that it can be turned in any direction.
Students fold a paper on the tool to make a straight angle, a right angle and a perpendicular crease, and find right angles on a grid and in the classroom.
Students sort angles into three groups by comparing each with a right angle, and name the groups acute, right and obtuse.
Students identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in figures, draw some in different orientations, say why the words acute and obtuse were chosen, and count acute angles in a pattern.
Students say that the angle measure is the number of 1° unit parts, and give the measure of a full turn, a straight angle and a right angle.
Students find the angle at the centre when a circle is cut into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 or 12 equal parts, and see why 360 is a handy number.
Students state that a full turn is 360 degrees, a straight angle is 180 degrees and a right angle is 90 degrees, and find the angle for equal cuts of a circle.
Students say why a protractor has two sets of numbers and count 1° units on an unlabelled one.
Students name every angle at a vertex with its measure, and find an angle between two arms by subtracting their two readings.
Students place the protractor centre on the vertex, set one arm on the 0 mark, and read the other arm directly.
Students count the 1° units between two arms on an unlabelled protractor, using 5s and 10s.
Students fold a circle into a semicircle and a quarter circle and work out 180° and 90° from the full turn.
Students fold again to get 45° and 22.5°, and say why all eight equal angles on the straight angle are 22.5° each.
Students name a fold that halves an angle as an angle bisector, and find the angle bisectors in the folded paper semicircle.
Students fold a paper semicircle on the tool and place the marks 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°, 112.5°, 135°, 157.5° and 180°.
Students find what went wrong in a student's protractor reading, say which check was missed, and mend the reading.
Students place the protractor on angles of different sizes and directions and read each one, find the angles in a classroom, and check that the three angles of a triangle add to 180°.
Students find the angle between the clock hands at an hour by splitting 360° into 12 equal parts.
Students find angles in clocks, a door, a swing, a toy and a rotated picture, and give each as a turn in degrees.
Students draw a given angle, such as ∠TIN of 30°, with a protractor, by marking the measure and joining.
Students guess and check angle sizes in two team games, and see how a good estimate comes from remembering 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°.
Students list every angle in a figure, draw angles of given sizes, and copy an angle by measuring it.
Students name an angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight by comparing its measure with 90 and 180.
Students say that an angle bigger than a straight angle and less than a full turn is reflex, and find its measure from the part of the turn that is left.
Students use the 180° straight angle to find an unknown neighbouring angle by subtracting the given one.
Students measure or estimate angles, classify each, draw angles of given sizes and build figures and letters from angle clues.
Students recall how lines, rays and angles are named, how an angle is measured and drawn, and what each type of angle is.

Book item: Vidya wants to draw a 30° angle and name it ∠TIN using a protractor. In ∠TIN, I will be the vertex, IT and IN will be the arms of the angle. Keeping one arm, say IN, as the reference (base), the other arm IT should take a turn of 30°. Step 1: We begin with the base and draw ray IN. Step 2: We will place the centre point of the protractor on I and align IN to the 0 line. Step 3: Now, starting from 0, count your degrees (0, 10, 30) up to 30 on the protractor. Mark point T at the label 30°. Step 4: Using a ruler join the point I and T. ∠TIN = 30° is the required angle.

Book item: Angle guessing game with two teams. Team 1 secretly chooses an angle measure, for example 49°, and makes an angle with that measure using a protractor without Team 2 being able to see it. Team 2 now gets to look at the angle. They have to quickly discuss and guess the number of degrees in the angle (without using a protractor!). Team 1 now demonstrates the true measure of the angle with a protractor. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between their guess and the correct measure. For example, if Team 2 guesses 39°, then they score 10 points (49°−39°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is the team with the lowest score.

Book item: Same two teams, new rules. Team 1 announces to all an angle measure, e.g., 34°. A player from Team 2 must draw that angle on the board without using a protractor. Other members of Team 2 can help the player by speaking words like 'Make it bigger!' or 'Make it smaller!'. A player from Team 1 measures the angle with a protractor for all to see. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between Team 2's angle size and the intended angle size. For example, if the player's angle from Team 2 is measured to be 25°, then Team 2 scores 9 points (34°−25°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is again the team with the lowest score.
